REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2): DEADLINE FOR A SPONSOR TO NOTIFY FDA OF AN UNEXPECTED FATAL OR LIFE-THREATENING SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTION
Draft for review by a qualified clinician / regulatory reviewer. Not medical advice and not for patient care. Every statement below is tied to the regulation text quoted, to the FDA guidance quoted, or to a named source listed in Section 12.

=== 1. ANSWER (the determination) ===
A sponsor must notify FDA of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction AS SOON AS POSSIBLE, AND IN NO CASE LATER THAN 7 CALENDAR DAYS AFTER THE SPONSOR'S INITIAL RECEIPT OF THE INFORMATION.
- Figure: 7. Unit: calendar days. Anchor event (Day 0): the sponsor's initial receipt of the information. Recipient of the notification: FDA. Citation: 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2), as set out in the supplied eCFR text.
- "As soon as possible" is a separate, independently enforceable obligation that precedes the 7-calendar-day outer limit; the 7 days is a ceiling, not a target.
- This is distinct from, and in addition to, the 15-calendar-day IND safety report to FDA and all participating investigators under § 312.32(c)(1). See Section 3.

=== 2. GOVERNING TEXT, QUOTED VERBATIM FROM THE SUPPLIED eCFR TEXT ===
§ 312.32(c)(2) — Unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction reports (quoted exactly):
"The sponsor must also notify FDA of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible but in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information."
Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-312/subpart-B/section-312.32 (fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z; sha256 db41c60ea129). The same sentence appears word-for-word in the GovInfo 2025 print edition (CFR-2025-title21-vol5, 4-1-25 edition, sha256 25450092fab4) and the GovInfo 2022 XML (sha256 873c9373598d), and in the Part 312 page of eCFR (sha256 c9fcf5cc6176). Source note printed with the section: "[75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010]".

FDA's own restatement, consistent with the text (quoted):
"For unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions: Sponsors must notify FDA as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information. See 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2)."
Source: FDA, IND Application Reporting: IND Safety Reports, https://www.fda.gov/drugs/investigational-new-drug-application-ind/ind-application-reporting-ind-safety-reports (fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z; sha256 195331f9a6e1).

FDA guidance footnote (quoted):
"Note that if the unexpected suspected adverse reaction is fatal or life-threatening, the requirement is to notify FDA as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information (see § 312.32(c)(2)). As with all serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions, sponsors must report unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions to all participating investigators (see § 312.32(c)(1))."
Source: FDA guidance document at https://www.fda.gov/media/152530/download (fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z; sha256 c597c1d15d04), footnote 22. The fetched text describes itself as guidance for clinical investigators on IND safety reporting under § 312.64(b)/§ 312.66 and IDE reporting under § 812.150; the exact title and issuance date were not in the captured text and must be read off the title page before external citation.

=== 3. WHY 7 DAYS AND NOT 15 — THE TWO CLOCKS, KEPT SEPARATE ===
§ 312.32(c)(1) (quoted): "The sponsor must notify FDA and all participating investigators (i.e., all investigators to whom the sponsor is providing drug under its INDs or under any investigator's IND) in an IND safety report of potential serious risks, from clinical trials or any other source, as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines that the information qualifies for reporting under paragraph (c)(1)(i), (c)(1)(ii), (c)(1)(iii), or (c)(1)(iv) of this section."
Table of the three clocks in § 312.32 that a sponsor must not conflate:
| Obligation | Citation | Clock starts | Limit | Recipient |
| Fatal/life-threatening unexpected suspected adverse reaction — notification | § 312.32(c)(2) | Sponsor's initial receipt of the information | 7 calendar days (as soon as possible) | FDA |
| Serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction — IND safety report | § 312.32(c)(1), (c)(1)(i) | Sponsor's determination that the information qualifies for reporting | 15 calendar days (as soon as possible) | FDA and all participating investigators |
| Newly reportable event found on follow-up investigation | § 312.32(d)(3) | The determination is made | 15 calendar days (as soon as possible) | FDA and participating investigators (IND safety report) |
Consistency check: 7 calendar days < 15 calendar days, so the fatal/life-threatening notification can never be satisfied by filing within the 15-day (c)(1) window. The word "also" in (c)(2) makes the 7-day notification cumulative with, not a substitute for, the (c)(1) IND safety report; the guidance footnote quoted in Section 2 confirms the investigator-facing obligation runs through (c)(1).

=== 4. WHAT STARTS THE CLOCK — "INITIAL RECEIPT", NOT "DETERMINATION" ===
- The (c)(2) trigger is the sponsor's INITIAL RECEIPT OF THE INFORMATION. The (c)(1) trigger is the sponsor's DETERMINATION that the information qualifies for reporting. These are different events, and the (c)(2) clock starts earlier — it does not wait for causality assessment, for unblinding, for the investigator's written narrative, or for a safety committee's adjudication.
- The supplied text does not further define "initial receipt" (e.g., receipt by any sponsor personnel versus first knowledge by a safety officer), and no passage in the captured sources resolves that question. Operational position to be fixed in the sponsor's SOPs, labelled as an operational interpretation and not as regulation: the clock starts on the calendar date the information is first received by any sponsor personnel or any party acting for the sponsor (including a CRO or vendor), and that date/time and its source document are recorded in the safety database as Day 0.
- Time of day: the text specifies calendar days and gives no rule for partial days. Operational practice: treat the calendar date of receipt as Day 0 and transmit by the end of Day 7.
- Calendar days include Saturdays, Sundays and U.S. Federal holidays. No weekend/holiday extension appears anywhere in the supplied Part 312 text.

=== 5. WHAT THE REQUIREMENT COVERS — THE FOUR ELEMENTS ===
The notification is owed only when all four elements in (c)(2) are present: (i) the reaction is UNEXPECTED; (ii) it is FATAL OR LIFE-THREATENING; (iii) it is a SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTION; (iv) the sponsor holds an IND (the obligation in § 312.32 is imposed on the sponsor; investigators have separate obligations under § 312.64(b)).
Definitional language that the supplied text itself supplies for element (iii), § 312.32(c)(1)(i) (quoted): "The sponsor must report an adverse event as a suspected adverse reaction only if there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the adverse event, such as:" — i.e., a bare temporal association is not enough; there must be evidence suggesting causation.
Verification item: the formal definitions of "adverse event", "adverse reaction", "suspected adverse reaction", "serious", "unexpected", and "life-threatening" sit in § 312.32(a). The § 312.32(a) text was NOT among the passages captured from the supplied sources, so no (a) definition is quoted here; the reviewer should read the definitions from § 312.32(a) in the same eCFR version (sha256 db41c60ea129) before this determination is used to classify a specific case.
Scope note from § 312.32(c)(4) (quoted): "A sponsor of a clinical study of a drug marketed or approved in the United States that is conducted under an IND is required to submit IND safety reports for suspected adverse reactions that are observed in the clinical study, at domestic or foreign study sites." The 7-day clock therefore is not limited to domestic sites.
Study-endpoint note (quoted from the supplied CFR text): "However, if a serious and unexpected adverse event occurs for which there is evidence suggesting a causal relationship between the drug and the event (e.g., death from anaphylaxis), the event must be reported under §312.32(c)(1)(i) as a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction even if it is a component of the study endpoint (e.g., all-cause mortality)." A fatal event that is a protocol endpoint is not thereby exempt from the 7-day notification when the causal-evidence test is met.

=== 6. TO WHOM ===
- § 312.32(c)(2) names FDA only. The 7-calendar-day limit applies to the FDA notification.
- Participating investigators receive the report under § 312.32(c)(1) (15 calendar days after determination), per the guidance footnote quoted in Section 2. Do not represent the 7-day limit as an investigator-notification deadline; the text does not say that.

=== 7. HOW TO TRANSMIT — FORMAT AND ROUTING ===
Format/transmission sentence closing § 312.32(c)(1) in the supplied CFR text (quoted): "Each notification to FDA must bear prominent identification of its contents, i.e., 'IND Safety Report,' and must be transmitted to the review division in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research or in the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research that has responsibility for review of the IND."
Electronic submission: FDA's page states (quoted): "As of April 1, 2026, submission of IND safety reports of serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i) must be submitted to FDA electronically to the FDA Adverse Event Monitoring System (AEMS) database ... using E2B(R3) data standards via Database-to-Database Transmission or the Safety Reporting Portal. ... Note that noncommercial INDs (i.e., INDs for products not intended for commercial distribution, including investigator-sponsored INDs and expanded access INDs) are exempt from this requirement." Read carefully: the captured statement is expressly about § 312.32(c)(1)(i) reports and does not, in the captured text, address the § 312.32(c)(2) notification. Route confirmation for (c)(2) notifications should be obtained from the responsible review division and recorded in the SOP.
Variance authority — § 312.32(c)(3) (quoted): "FDA may require a sponsor to submit IND safety reports in a format or at a frequency different than that required under this paragraph. The sponsor may also propose and adopt a different reporting format or frequency if the change is agreed to in advance by the director of the FDA review division that has responsibility for review of the IND." Before applying the 7-calendar-day default, confirm in writing that no such advance agreement exists for the IND in question; if one exists, the agreed term governs.

=== 8. WHAT FOLLOWS THE NOTIFICATION ===
§ 312.32(d) (quoted):
(d)(1) "The sponsor must promptly investigate all safety information it receives."
(d)(2) "Relevant followup information to an IND safety report must be submitted as soon as the information is available and must be identified as such, i.e., 'Followup IND Safety Report.'"
(d)(3) "If the results of a sponsor's investigation show that an adverse event not initially determined to be reportable under paragraph (c) of this section is so reportable, the sponsor must report such suspected adverse reaction in an IND safety report as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after the determination is made."
Additional data on FDA request (quoted): "Upon request from FDA, the sponsor must submit to FDA any additional data or information that the agency deems necessary, as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request." (15 calendar days; distinct from the 7-calendar-day notification.)
Disclaimer preserved — § 312.32(e) (quoted): "A safety report or other information submitted by a sponsor under this part (and any release by FDA of that report or information) does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the sponsor or FDA that the report or information constitutes an admission that the drug caused or contributed to an adverse event. A sponsor need not admit, and may deny, that the report or information submitted by the sponsor constitutes an admission that the drug caused or contributed to an adverse event."

=== 9. CALENDAR ARITHMETIC — WORKED EXAMPLES (all figures in calendar days) ===
Rule: Deadline = date of the sponsor's initial receipt (Day 0) + 7 calendar days.
| Day 0 (initial receipt) | Day 0 weekday | Deadline (Day 0 + 7 calendar days) | Deadline weekday | Note |
| 2026-03-02 | Monday | 2026-03-09 | Monday | — |
| 2026-03-06 | Friday | 2026-03-13 | Friday | Weekend falls inside the window; no extension |
| 2026-12-24 | Thursday | 2026-12-31 | Thursday | Christmas Day (2026-12-25) falls inside the window; no extension in the supplied text |
Internal target (operational recommendation, not a regulatory requirement): transmit the FDA notification well inside the 7-day ceiling, because "as soon as possible" is enforceable independently of the 7-day limit; a 24–72 hour internal target with the Day 0 date/time recorded in the safety database is consistent with the text while leaving margin for the 7-day outer limit.

=== 10. CONSEQUENCES OF LATE OR MISSING NOTIFICATION ===
Quoted from the supplied Part 312 text (termination ground): "The sponsor fails promptly to investigate and inform the Food and Drug Administration and all investigators of serious and unexpected adverse experiences in accordance with § 312.32 or fails to make any other report required under this part."
Related safety-action provision quoted from the supplied Part 312 text: "A sponsor who determines that its investigational drug presents an unreasonable and significant risk to subjects shall discontinue those investigations that present the risk, notify FDA, all institutional review boards, and all investigators who have at any time participated in the investigation of the discontinuance, assure the disposition of all stocks of the drug outstanding as required by § 312.59, and furnish FDA with a full report of the sponsor's actions. The sponsor shall discontinue the investigation as soon as possible, and in no event later than 5 working days after making the determination that the investigation should be discontinued." (5 working days — a different obligation from the 7-calendar-day notification; do not merge the two.)
Citation integrity note: these two Part 312 statements were captured without section numbers; before external use, confirm them as § 312.44(b) (grounds for termination) and § 312.56(d) (discontinuation of investigation) respectively in the same eCFR version (sha256 db41c60ea129).

=== 11. RELATED REQUIREMENTS OUTSIDE § 312.32(c)(2) — DO NOT SUBSTITUTE ===
- Investigator to sponsor, § 312.64(b) (quoted): "The investigator must immediately report to the sponsor any serious adverse event, whether or not considered drug-related, including those listed in the protocol or investigator brochure, as well as an assessment of whether there is a reasonable possibility that the drug caused the event (§ 312.64(b))." FDA guidance on "immediately" (quoted): "the Agency interprets immediately to be as soon as feasible after the investigator recognizes an event is an SAE and obtains relevant information for the sponsor" and "FDA recommends that this time frame for submitting such initial information also be specified in the protocol and anticipates that the time frame for submission of initial information will generally not exceed 1 calendar day." (1 calendar day — an investigator-facing recommendation, not the sponsor's 7-day obligation; a delay upstream of the sponsor shortens, but never lengthens, the sponsor's 7 calendar days.)
- IND-exempt bioavailability/bioequivalence studies, § 320.31(d)(3), as described in the FDA guidance (quoted): "the person conducting the study, including any contract research organization, must notify FDA and all participating investigators of any serious adverse event [SAE] ... as soon as possible but in no case later than 15 calendar days after becoming aware of its occurrence" and must notify FDA of any "fatal or life-threatening adverse event from the study as soon as possible but in no case later than 7 calendar days after becoming aware" of its occurrence. Same 7-calendar-day figure, different anchor wording ("becoming aware") and different regulatory part — keep the two citations separate.
- Device studies (IDE, § 812.150) have their own timelines (e.g., 10 working days) and are outside this determination.

=== 12. SOURCES CITED IN FULL, WITH VERSION ===
1. 21 CFR 312.32 — Indications of a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction; IND safety reports. eCFR, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 312, Subpart B. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-312/subpart-B/section-312.32 — fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z, sha256 db41c60ea129. Section source note: 75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010.
2. 21 CFR Part 312 (part-level page, same eCFR). https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-312 — fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:43Z, sha256 c9fcf5cc6176.
3. Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Volume 5, § 312.32, 4-1-25 edition (print). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol5-sec312-32.pdf — fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z, sha256 25450092fab4.
4. Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Volume 5, § 312.32, 2022 XML. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2022-title21-vol5/xml/CFR-2022-title21-vol5-sec312-32.xml — fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z, sha256 873c9373598d.
5. FDA, IND Application Reporting: IND Safety Reports (web page). https://www.fda.gov/drugs/investigational-new-drug-application-ind/ind-application-reporting-ind-safety-reports — fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z, sha256 195331f9a6e1.
6. FDA guidance document (investigator safety reporting; IND § 312.64(b)/§ 312.66 and IDE § 812.150), https://www.fda.gov/media/152530/download — fetched 2026-11-23T04:03:42Z, sha256 c597c1d15d04; footnote dated (December 2025) in the captured text; confirm title/issuance date from the title page.
Version-stability check performed: the operative § 312.32(c)(2) sentence is word-identical across sources 1, 3 and 4 (eCFR current, CFR 2025 print, CFR 2022 XML). The answer therefore does not depend on which of the supplied versions is used. If the requester needs the regulation as of a specific historical date not covered by these three versions, that date must be supplied and re-checked; nothing in the supplied set suggests any change in (c)(2) between 2022 and the current eCFR.

=== 13. HOW TO APPLY THIS IN ONE LINE ===
On the calendar date the sponsor first receives information indicating an unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction, record that date as Day 0, notify FDA as soon as possible, and in every case transmit the notification by the end of Day 0 + 7 calendar days, with the IND safety report to FDA and all participating investigators following under § 312.32(c)(1) within 15 calendar days of the sponsor's determination that the information qualifies for reporting.

=== 14. OPEN ITEMS FOR THE REVIEWER (verification, not gaps in the answer) ===
1. Read the § 312.32(a) definitions of "serious", "unexpected", "life-threatening", "suspected adverse reaction" in the same eCFR version (sha256 db41c60ea129) before applying the four-element test in Section 5 to a specific case; those definitions were not in the captured passages and are not quoted here.
2. Confirm whether any § 312.32(c)(3) advance agreement on format/frequency exists for the IND in question; if so, the agreed term governs instead of the 7-calendar-day default.
3. Confirm the citation numbers for the termination ground and the 5-working-day discontinuation provision (Section 10) from the full Part 312 text.
4. Confirm the current transmission route for § 312.32(c)(2) notifications with the responsible review division, given that the captured electronic-submission statement addresses § 312.32(c)(1)(i) reports only.
5. Fix in the sponsor's SOP the operational definition of "initial receipt" (Section 4), which the supplied text leaves undefined.

# Submission lead time for a premarket notification (510(k)) under 21 CFR Part 807, subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21

Draft for review by a qualified regulatory professional. Not regulatory advice; not a filing decision. Every statement below is tied to a cited provision, and the population, the trigger and the units are stated with each figure.

## 1. Answer

**At least 90 days.** A person required to register its establishment under 21 CFR 807.20 who must submit a premarket notification for a device intended for human use must submit that notification to FDA **at least 90 calendar days before** the person proposes to begin the **introduction, or delivery for introduction, into interstate commerce for commercial distribution** of the device.

- Figure: 90.
- Units: days (calendar days; the regulation states a floor — "at least").
- Trigger event: the proposed *beginning of* introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution — not the date of clearance, not the date of first sale, not the date of manufacturing.
- Population: each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20.
- Governing provision: 21 CFR 807.81(a).

## 2. Governing text, quoted in full

21 CFR 807.81 — *When a premarket notification submission is required*:

> "(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:
>
> (1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to,
>   (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or
>   (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.
> (2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.
> (3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:
>   (i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.
>   (ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.
>
> (b)(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:
>   (i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or
>   (ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.
> (2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.
> (c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter."
>
> Source note: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024]"

Retrieved from the eCFR at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E/section-807.81 (fetch 2026-11-23T04:07:15Z, sha256 cffa5dd519c4), with the same operative sentence reproduced on the subpart E index page and the Part 807 page (sha256 c74dcd356a8a and 40bacc3a23f9 respectively).

## 3. What the answer does and does not depend on

| Variable | Effect on the 90-day figure | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Role of the person (manufacturer, specification developer, initial importer, repackager, relabeler) | **None**, once the person is within the class "required to register … pursuant to § 807.20." Role affects *whether* a person is in that class; it does not alter the lead time. | § 807.81(a) applies uniformly to "each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20." |
| Which criterion is triggered — (a)(1), (a)(2) or (a)(3) | **None.** All three are governed by the single 90-day clause in the introductory text of (a). | § 807.81(a) introductory text. |
| Device class (I, II or III) | **None**, provided the device requires premarket notification and no exemption or exception applies. | § 807.81(a); see rows below. |
| Device-specific classification regulation | Subpart E contains **no** mechanism by which a classification regulation shortens or lengthens this lead time. The only timing provision in subpart E is § 807.81(a). | Subpart E, §§ 807.81–807.100. |
| § 807.81(b)(1)(i) — PMA or 513(f)(2) reclassification petition pending | **Not applicable / no lead time arises**: a premarket notification is *not required*. This removes the obligation; it does not shorten the clock. | § 807.81(b)(1)(i). |
| § 807.81(b)(1)(ii) — PCCP cleared under section 515C, change consistent with the PCCP | **Not applicable / no lead time arises** for that change: a premarket notification is *not required*. | § 807.81(b)(1)(ii). |
| § 807.81(b)(2) — Center Director determination that a granted exception/alternative request under § 801.128 or § 809.11 satisfies (a)(3) | **Not applicable / no lead time arises** for the (a)(3) change, if and when the Center Director so determines. | § 807.81(b)(2). |
| § 807.85(a) — custom device within section 520(b) of the FD&C Act | **Exempt from premarket notification**: no submission and therefore no lead time. | 21 CFR 807.85(a); source note "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016]". |
| § 807.85(b) — distributor placing a device into commercial distribution for the first time under its own name, and repackager placing its own name on a device without changing other labeling, where the device was in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or a notification was filed by another person | **Exempt from premarket notification**: no lead time. | 21 CFR 807.85(b)(1)–(2). |
| FDA guidance or review practice | **No effect.** Guidance does not amend § 807.81(a). FDA's review-time goals are a separate matter and do not modify the regulatory lead time. | § 807.81(a) is the operative text; guidance is not a regulation. |

Two figures that are *not* the lead time and must not be conflated with it:

- **90 days** in § 807.95 confidentiality provisions — "90 days from the date of receipt of the submission" — is a non-disclosure period measured *from receipt*, not a pre-marketing lead time.
- **30 days** in § 807.87(h) practice ("If the additional information is not submitted within 30 days following the date of the request, the Commissioner will consider the premarket notification to be withdrawn") is a response window after an FDA request, not a pre-marketing lead time.

## 4. Version control — "as in force on 2026-11-21"

1. The eCFR text was retrieved on **2026-11-23T04:07:15Z**, two days after the date of interest.
2. The source note of § 807.81 lists amendment history ending at **89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024**. No later amendment to § 807.81 appears in that source note, and the operative sentence in the retrieved text still reads "at least 90 days."
3. The 2024 amendment (89 FR 18792) appears in the source note alongside the § 807.81(b)(1)(ii) PCCP carve-out; the 90-day period in § 807.81(a) is unchanged in the retrieved text.
4. **Conclusion:** on the retrieved text, the lead time in force on 2026-11-21 is 90 days.
5. **Residual verification step for the reviewer** (not a reason to withhold the answer): confirm against the eCFR "Changes to 21 CFR Part 807" / Federal Register listing that no document with an effective date in the window 2024-03-15 through 2026-11-21 amended § 807.81(a), and confirm that no document effective 2026-11-22 through 2026-11-23 (the two-day gap between the date of interest and the fetch) altered it. If either check finds an amendment, re-derive the figure from the amended text before use.

## 5. Worked date computation (units: calendar days)

Method: proposed first introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce = D. Latest submission date = D − 90 calendar days. The regulation states calendar days and provides no business-day adjustment.

Worked example: D = 2027-03-01.

- 2027-03-01 − 28 days = 2027-02-01 (February 2027 has 28 days; 2027 is not a leap year).
- 2027-02-01 − 31 days = 2027-01-01 (running total 59 days).
- 2027-01-01 − 31 days = 2026-12-01 (running total 90 days).
- **Latest submission date = 2026-12-01** for a proposed 2027-03-01 introduction.

Operational note for the reviewer, outside subpart E: because 90 days is a floor and FDA's acceptance of a submission depends on matters such as the user fee and a complete submission under § 807.87, planning should target a date earlier than D − 90 rather than exactly D − 90. Those matters are governed elsewhere and do not change the 90-day regulatory minimum.

## 6. Reviewer verification checklist

- [ ] Confirm § 807.81(a) in the eCFR text effective 2026-11-21 still reads "at least 90 days."
- [ ] Confirm the person is within the class "required to register … pursuant to § 807.20" (this is a § 807.20 determination, outside subpart E).
- [ ] Confirm the device requires premarket notification under § 807.81(a)(1), (a)(2) or (a)(3).
- [ ] Confirm none of § 807.81(b)(1)(i), (b)(1)(ii) or (b)(2) applies.
- [ ] Confirm neither § 807.85(a) nor § 807.85(b) exempts the device or the person.
- [ ] Confirm the planned commercial-distribution date and compute D − 90 in calendar days.
- [ ] Confirm the definition of "commercial distribution" applicable to the trigger under 21 CFR 807.3 (subpart A definitions) before fixing D.

## 7. Limitations of this draft

- It answers the timing question only. It does not determine whether a particular device requires a 510(k), which depends on classification and on § 807.81(a)(1)–(3) applied to the specific device.
- It does not address § 807.87 content requirements, § 807.93/§ 807.94 certifications, the 510(k) user fee, or the separate question of when marketing may lawfully begin after submission.

# IRB/IEC Composition under ICH E6(R2): Minimum Recommended Membership and the Two Required Member Characteristics

**Status of this document.** Draft evidence extract prepared for review by a qualified clinician / regulatory reviewer. It is not medical advice and is not for patient care. It records what the guideline text says; it does not substitute for an institution's written IRB/IEC operating procedures or for the applicable national regulatory requirements.

---

## 1. Questions addressed

- **(2)** Under ICH E6(R2), what minimum total membership is recommended for an IRB/IEC?
- **(3)** Which two membership characteristics should be included?

---

## 2. Governing source and version

**Primary source (governs the answer).**
ICH. *ICH Harmonised Guideline: Guideline for Good Clinical Practice E6(R2)*. ICH E6(R2), Step 5. Document EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995. European Medicines Agency, 1 November 2016 (Step 5 adoption by the ICH Steering Committee, 9 November 2016). Section 3.2 "Composition, Functions, and Operations", paragraph 3.2.1, page 21/75 (PDF line numbers 552–561). https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-guideline-good-clinical-practice-e6r2-step-5-revision-2_en.pdf — fetched 2026-11-23T04:10:18Z, SHA-256 prefix c9bc99c11937.

**Corroborating source (same operative wording).**
US Food and Drug Administration. *E6(R2) Good Clinical Practice: Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1) — Guidance for Industry*. Section 3.2.1, page 13. https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/E6(R2)-Good-Clinical-Practice_-Integrated-Addendum-to-ICH-E6(R1)-_-Guidance-for-Industry.pdf — fetched 2026-11-23T04:10:18Z, SHA-256 prefix 6e427d45ecd5.

**Version note.** E6(R2) is an integrated addendum to E6(R1). Section 3.2.1 is carried unchanged into the integrated text: the wording quoted in Section 3 below is identical in the EMA Step 5 PDF and in the FDA-published integrated addendum, both of which were checked for this draft. The answer below therefore applies to ICH E6(R2) as adopted at Step 5 and to the FDA's published integrated addendum of the same guideline.

---

## 3. Operative text (verbatim, ICH E6(R2) Section 3.2.1)

> "3.2.1 The IRB/IEC should consist of a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial. It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include:
>
> (a) At least five members.
>
> (b) At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area.
>
> (c) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.
>
> Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter.
>
> A list of IRB/IEC members and their qualifications should be maintained."

Source: ICH E6(R2), EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995, Section 3.2.1, page 21/75 (lines 552–561); identical in FDA integrated addendum, Section 3.2.1, page 13.

---

## 4. Answers

### 4.1 (Ask 2) Minimum total membership recommended: **five members**

- **Figure:** 5
- **Unit:** members (headcount on the IRB/IEC roster)
- **Basis:** ICH E6(R2) Section 3.2.1(a) — verbatim: "At least five members."
- **Population / scope:** the composition of the IRB/IEC itself (the reviewing body), not the trial population and not the number of members present at a meeting.
- **Strength of the statement:** the guideline uses "It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include" and "At least five members." Five is therefore a **recommended floor** for the composition of the committee, expressed as a minimum ("at least"). It is not phrased as a statutory requirement, and it is not a quorum.
- **Interaction with the first sentence of 3.2.1:** the committee must also be of "a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial." Five is the stated recommended minimum count; it does not by itself discharge the collective-qualification requirement, so a roster of exactly five that lacks coverage of the science, medical or ethics dimension would still not meet 3.2.1 as a whole.

### 4.2 (Ask 3) The two membership characteristics to be included

The two characteristics are items **(b)** and **(c)** of Section 3.2.1. Item (a) is a headcount, not a membership characteristic, and is therefore not one of the two.

| # | Verbatim text (ICH E6(R2) 3.2.1) | What it requires | Minimum count implied | How it is evidenced |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (b) | "At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area." | At least one member whose **primary** area of interest is nonscientific (e.g., law, ethics, lay/consumer perspective, ministry of health or other non-scientific discipline). The test attaches to the member's primary area of interest, not to a secondary interest or hobby. | 1 member | Membership list annotated with each member's primary area of interest (3.2.1 last sentence; 3.3.1) |
| (c) | "At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site." | At least one member with **no affiliation to the institution or the trial site** — i.e., a member who is not part of the institution or site conducting the trial. | 1 member | Membership list annotated with institutional/site affiliation status (3.2.1 last sentence; 3.3.1) |

**Answer as a single identifier:** ICH E6(R2) 3.2.1(b) — at least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area; and ICH E6(R2) 3.2.1(c) — at least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.

---

## 5. Boundaries of the answer — four points that must not be conflated

**5.1 Item (a) is not a "membership characteristic."** Section 3.2.1 lists three bullets. Bullet (a) fixes a headcount (five members); bullets (b) and (c) fix attributes of at least one member each. The "two membership characteristics" are (b) and (c). Counting (a) as a characteristic would be a misreading of the list.

**5.2 Membership is not quorum.** Section 3.2.3 (verbatim): "An IRB/IEC should make its decisions at announced meetings at which at least a quorum, as stipulated in its written operating procedures, is present." E6(R2) fixes **no** numeric quorum; the number is set in the IRB/IEC's own written operating procedures. The figure of five members in 3.2.1(a) must not be reported as a quorum.

**5.3 Independence from the institution/trial site (c) is not the same test as voting independence.** The second paragraph of 3.2.1 states: "Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter." This is a **broader** independence test (independence from the *investigator* and the *sponsor*) than item (c) (independence from the *institution/trial site*). A member can satisfy (c) and still be excluded from voting on a given trial because of a relationship to the investigator or sponsor. Both provisions must be reflected in the roster and in the conflict-of-interest procedure.

**5.4 Diversity-of-composition language is not in E6(R2) Section 3.2.1.** Requirements for a committee with varying backgrounds and diversity of composition (including race, gender and cultural background), and for a member not otherwise affiliated with the institution, come from other frameworks — for example US 21 CFR 56.107 ("IRB membership") under 21 CFR Part 56. Those are **comparators, not the governing text for this question**, and are cited here only to prevent conflation. *Caution: the 21 CFR 56.107 wording has not been re-verified verbatim against the current eCFR for this draft; confirm the version in force on eCFR before any external reliance.* Where a trial falls under both ICH E6(R2) and a national regime, the more demanding applicable requirement governs the committee's composition in practice.

---

## 6. How to evidence compliance in a protocol / IRB submission package

1. **Membership list with names and qualifications**, annotated to show, per member, the primary area of interest and institutional/site affiliation — satisfying 3.2.1 last sentence ("A list of IRB/IEC members and their qualifications should be maintained") and 3.3.1 ("Determining its composition (names and qualifications of the members) and the authority under which it is established"). The annotations are what make items (b) and (c) auditable rather than asserted.
2. **Written operating procedures** covering composition, scheduling and conduct of meetings, initial and continuing review, and frequency of continuing review — 3.2.2 and 3.3.
3. **Quorum rule** stated in those operating procedures — 3.2.3.
4. **Conflict-of-interest / voting rule** implementing the second paragraph of 3.2.1 (independence from investigator and sponsor) and 3.2.4 (only members who participate in review and discussion vote) and 3.2.5 (the investigator may provide information but does not deliberate or vote).
5. **Sponsor-side documentation**: the name and address of the investigator's/institution's IRB/IEC; a statement from the IRB/IEC that it is organised and operates according to GCP and applicable laws and regulations; and documented, dated approval/favourable opinion — from the sponsor-obligation passage in E6(R2) Section 5.11 ("Confirmation of Review by IRB/IEC") as quoted in the source set for this draft. *Sub-section number to be re-confirmed against the Step 5 PDF pagination before external use.*

---

## 7. Limits of this draft

- The answer states a **recommendation** in a guideline, not a legal minimum in any particular jurisdiction. National implementations may impose additional or different requirements; the applicable regulatory requirement(s) must be checked for each trial (see E6(R2) Section 3.2.2, which requires the IRB/IEC to comply with GCP **and** with the applicable regulatory requirement(s)).
- The guideline text in Section 3 was reproduced from the fetched PDFs identified in Section 2 (SHA-256 prefixes given for traceability). Before this note is used outside internal review, the quoted text should be checked character-for-character against the controlled copy of the Step 5 PDF held by the organisation.
- The Section 5.11 sub-number and the 21 CFR 56.107 comparator flagged in Sections 5.4 and 6 are the two items in this draft requiring re-verification.

---

## 8. Sources cited in full

1. ICH. *ICH Harmonised Guideline: Guideline for Good Clinical Practice E6(R2)*. ICH E6(R2), Step 5. EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995. European Medicines Agency, 1 November 2016. Section 3.2.1 (page 21/75); Section 3.2.3; Section 3.2.4; Section 3.2.5; Section 3.3.1. https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-guideline-good-clinical-practice-e6r2-step-5-revision-2_en.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T04:10:18Z; SHA-256 prefix c9bc99c11937).
2. US Food and Drug Administration. *E6(R2) Good Clinical Practice: Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1) — Guidance for Industry*. Section 3.2.1, page 13. https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/E6(R2)-Good-Clinical-Practice_-Integrated-Addendum-to-ICH-E6(R1)-_-Guidance-for-Industry.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T04:10:18Z; SHA-256 prefix 6e427d45ecd5).
3. US Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Part 56, Subpart C, §56.107 "IRB membership" (comparator only; not re-verified verbatim for this draft — confirm the version in force on eCFR before reliance).

---

## 9. One-line answer for the reviewer

Under ICH E6(R2) Section 3.2.1, the recommended minimum total membership of an IRB/IEC is **five members** (3.2.1(a), "At least five members"), and the two membership characteristics to be included are **at least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area** (3.2.1(b)) and **at least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site** (3.2.1(c)).

> “After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures the induration (firm swelling) where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative.”

**PDF fact sheet [4]:**

> “After two or three days, you must return to the clinic to have the skin test read. A trained health care provider will measure the size of the bump or reaction.”

**Ask 2 — When must the TST reaction be examined?**
**48 to 72 hours after administration** (unit: hours after intradermal placement of 0.1 mL PPD). The reaction must be examined within that window; CDC's operational corollary is that a patient who does not return within 72 hours must be rescheduled for another skin test [2][4]. The window is identical across the primary page [1], the TST subpage [2], the LTBI overview [3] and the PDF fact sheet [4]; the patient page's “two or three days” [5] is the same window stated less precisely. CDC's primary page does not give a separate instruction for a reading taken before 48 hours — do not infer one from this page.

**Ask 3 — Who must examine it?**
**A trained health care worker** — the primary page's wording [1], which also states results “should only be read by a trained health care professional” [1]. Equivalently, on CDC's TST subpage and fact sheet: “a health care worker trained to read TB skin results” [2][4], and, for placement and reading together, “a designated, trained health care provider” [2]. In all CDC variants the reader must be **trained**; **which** trained persons are authorised to place and read is set by state and local public health authorities, and CDC expressly directs the reader to consult them [1][2]. No CDC source on these pages permits an untrained reader or patient self-reading.

**Technique that goes with the reading (from [2][4], not stated on the primary page):** the reaction is measured in **millimetres of induration** (firm swelling), **not** erythema (redness), with the diameter measured across the forearm perpendicular to the long axis.

- **Evidence level.** The 48–72 hour window and the trained-reader requirement are CDC programmatic guidance from the Division of Tuberculosis Elimination [1–5]. The primary page cites no trial, systematic review or formal graded guideline for either element; it is guidance-level (standard-of-practice), not trial-level, evidence. This should be described that way in any downstream document.
- **Wording inconsistency, not substantive conflict.** “trained health care worker” [1][3], “trained health care professional” [1], “health care worker trained to read TB skin results” [2][4], “designated, trained health care provider” [2]. All variants require training; “designated” appears only in [2] and is the closest CDC comes to naming an appointment/authorisation process. No variant contradicts another on timing or on the training requirement.
- **Thin spot — measurement method.** The primary page [1] states only that the worker measures “any swelling”; the induration-not-erythema rule and the transverse-axis rule appear on the linked subpage [2] and the PDF [4]. If a downstream document must be confined strictly to the primary page, the measurement-technique statements fall outside that scope; the timing and reader statements do not.
- **Thin spot — the 48-hour lower bound.** CDC states the window's start but does not state what to do with a reading taken before 48 hours. No instruction is invented here.
- **Thin spot — authorisation.** CDC does not name which professions may read a TST; it delegates to state and local public health authorities [1][2]. Any statement that a specific profession (e.g., nurse, pharmacist, medical assistant) is or is not authorised is outside CDC's text.
- **Different test, different logistics.** Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) requires a single blood draw and no return visit for reading [4]; the 48–72 hour reading window applies to the TST only and must not be transferred to IGRA.
- **No numeric conflict.** The only figures in the timing rule are 48 h and 72 h; the rescheduling rule uses 72 h, the window's upper bound, and is consistent with it. TST interpretation cut-offs (5/10/15 mm induration, on [2]) are a separate question and are deliberately not used here.

## 6. Populations and circumstances CDC flags on these same pages (context only — not new answers)

- **Children younger than 5 years:** CDC guidelines recommend the TST as the testing method, noting some experts use IGRA; AAP guidance may be consulted [1].
- **BCG-vaccinated persons:** IGRA preferred, because BCG can cause a false-positive TST [3][4].
- **Persons unlikely to return for a reading:** IGRA preferred — a direct consequence of the mandatory 48–72 hour return [3].
- **Prior severe reaction to a TST:** contraindication to repeating the test [2].
- **Recent live-virus vaccination** (measles, mumps, rubella, oral polio, varicella, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid): TST either the same day or at least 1 month after [4].
- **Symptoms of TB disease:** do not wait for the TST result before starting other diagnostic tests [2].
- **Routine testing with both IGRA and TST is not recommended** [3].

1. Confirm “48–72 hours” is expressed in **hours after placement**, not days, and that the 72-hour upper bound matches the rescheduling rule quoted in §3.
2. Confirm the reader-qualification wording against your jurisdiction's public health regulations, since CDC defers authorisation to state and local authorities [1][2].
3. Confirm the measurement convention: millimetres of induration, transverse to the long axis of the forearm, erythema not measured [2][4].
4. Confirm the page version. If a byte-level capture dated 2026-11-21 is required, pull the archived copy and re-verify the two key sentences in §3 before the document is finalised.

# ICH E2A seven-day expedited reporting: outer notification limit and follow-up deadline

**Status: draft for review by a qualified clinician / regulatory affairs professional. Not medical advice. Not for patient care.**

---

## 1. Answers

**Ask 1 — outer limit for notifying regulatory agencies.**

> **7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies (i.e. on or before day 7, with day 0 = the date of first knowledge).**

Unit: calendar days. The notification is to be made *as soon as possible*; 7 calendar days is the outer limit, not a target. Permitted channels per the guideline text are "e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing".

**Ask 2 — follow-up report "as complete as possible" if the full 7-day period is used.**

> **Day 15 measured from day 0** (7 calendar days for the initial notification + 8 additional calendar days = 15 calendar days from day 0).

Unit: calendar days. Arithmetic: 7 + 8 = 15. If the initial notification is sent on day 7, the follow-up is due by day 15; day 15 is also the total elapsed window from day 0 (day 0 + 15 calendar days).

---

## 2. Governing text, quoted in full with source and version

**Source:** ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline, *Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting*, ICH topic E2A, Step 4 (recommended for adoption 27 October 1994); EU adoption reference **CPMP/ICH/377/95**, legal effective date **1 June 1995** (European Medicines Agency scientific-guideline page, first published 1 June 1995). Full text consulted as hosted by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (URL and retrieval date in §10).

**Operative passage (E2A §3.2 "Reporting Time Frames", numbered item 1 — fatal or life-threatening, unexpected ADRs occurring in clinical investigations):**

> "Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. This report should include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products."

**Contrasting passage (E2A §3.2, numbered item 2 — all other serious, unexpected ADRs):**

> "Serious, unexpected reactions (ADRs) that are not fatal or life-threatening must be filed as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case meets the minimum criteria for expedited reporting."

**Minimum criteria (E2A §3.2, numbered item 3):**

> "...initial reports should be submitted within the prescribed time as long as the following minimum criteria are met: an identifiable patient; a suspect medicinal product; an identifiable reporting source; and an event or outcome that can be identified as serious and unexpected, and for which, in clinical investigation cases, there is [a reasonable possibility that the event was caused by the medicinal product]."

*Note on the quotation:* the fetched passage terminates at "there is"; the bracketed completion is the standard continuation of the E2A sentence and should be checked against the printed guideline before the draft is finalised. The four listed minimum criteria themselves are quoted verbatim.

---

## 3. Population and case qualification (the answers only apply to this population)

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Product status | Investigational (pre-approval) — E2A is expressly the investigational-phase standard; its scope statement notes that premarketing and post-marketing concepts are "interdependent" |
| Reaction | Fatal **or** life-threatening, unexpected adverse drug reaction |
| Causality | Suspected — in clinical investigation cases, a reasonable possibility that the event was caused by the medicinal product |
| Minimum data | Identifiable patient; suspect medicinal product; identifiable reporting source; event identifiable as serious and unexpected |
| Clock start | First knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies |

The 7 + 8 day structure in ask 1 applies **only** to the fatal/life-threatening unexpected category. A serious, unexpected ADR that is *not* fatal or life-threatening falls under item 2 and has a single 15-calendar-day outer limit with no 7-day first step. Both routes land on day 15, which is a useful internal consistency check on the arithmetic in §1.

---

## 4. Day counting and the day-0 convention

- **Day 0** = the calendar date on which the sponsor first has knowledge that the case qualifies (i.e. the date the minimum criteria are met). Day 0 is **not** counted as day 1; the count of 7 begins the following calendar day.
- **Calendar days**, not business days: weekends and public holidays do not extend either deadline.
- The E2A text as fetched specifies "calendar days after first knowledge" but does not itself spell out the day-0 convention. The explicit convention is stated in the ICH **E2D** text consulted: *"The regulatory reporting time clock (in calendar days) starts on the date when any personnel of the MAH first receive a case report that fulfills minimum criteria as well as the criteria for expedited reporting. In general, this date should be considered as day 0."* (ICH E2D, §3.2.2 "Time Clock Start Point"; document footer "E2D ver3.8 (2003JUL18)", distributed on the FDA guidance site as a **draft** — January 2025 update. Because this is a draft, the day-0 convention is stated here as the operative sponsor convention, not as final E2A text.)
- Note also from the same E2D draft, §3.2.2: *"When additional medically significant information is received for a previously reported case, the regulatory reporting time clock begins again for submission of the follow-up report."* This is a separate trigger from the 8-additional-day rule and does not change the day-15 answer; it can make a follow-up due earlier if significant new information arrives sooner.
- **Conservative reading applied here:** the 8 additional days run from the end of the 7-day window (day 0 + 15), not from the actual date the initial notification was transmitted. A sponsor that notifies on day 2 should not plan on a day-10 follow-up; plan to day 15.

---

## 5. Worked timeline (all figures in calendar days from day 0)

| # | Milestone | Day from day 0 | Example (day 0 = Mon 3 Mar 2025) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | First knowledge; minimum criteria met; clock starts | 0 | Mon 3 Mar 2025 |
| 2 | Initial notification to regulatory agencies — outer limit | **7** | Mon 10 Mar 2025 |
| 3 | Follow-up report "as complete as possible" — outer limit | **15** | Tue 18 Mar 2025 |

Arithmetic verification: 3 Mar 2025 + 7 days = 10 Mar 2025; 10 Mar 2025 + 8 days = 18 Mar 2025; 3 Mar 2025 + 15 days = 18 Mar 2025. The two routes to the follow-up date agree. No weekend or holiday adjustment is applied to either date.

---

## 6. What the initial notification and the follow-up must contain

E2A is explicit that the initial report may be sent on minimum criteria alone: *"Information for final description and evaluation of a case report may not be available within the required time frames for reporting outlined above. Nevertheless, for regulatory purposes, initial reports should be submitted within the prescribed time as long as the following minimum criteria are met..."*

On format, E2A states: *"The CIOMS-I form has been a widely accepted standard for expedited adverse event reporting. However, no matter what the form or format used, it is important that certain basic information/data elements, when available, be included with any expedited report, whether in a tabular or narrative presentation."* The administrative/sponsor elements E2A lists include, verbatim:

> "Source of report: Was it spontaneous, from a clinical investigation (provide details), from the literature (provide copy), other?
> Date event report was first received by sponsor/manufacturer,
> Country in which event occurred,
> Type of report filed to authorities: initial or follow-up (first, second, etc.),
> Name and address of sponsor/manufacturer/company,
> Name, address, telephone number, and FAX number of contact person in reporting company or institution,
> Identifying regulatory code or number for marketing authorization dossier or clinical investigation process for the suspected product (for example IND or CTX number, NDA number),
> Sponsor/manufacturer's identification number for the case (This number should be the same for the initial and follow-up reports on the same case)."

Operational consequence: the initial 7-day notification is a valid, complete submission if it carries the four minimum criteria plus the administrative block above, and the follow-up submitted by day 15 must carry the full case (narrative, event details, reporter details, sponsor assessment of importance and implication, relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products). Use the identical sponsor case identification number on both, and label the second submission as a follow-up.

---

## 7. Jurisdictional overrides that must be checked before the draft is used

The 7/15 answers above are the **ICH E2A** answers. They are not automatically the operative legal deadlines in every region, and the following must be resolved for the specific case:

- **United States.** The FDA-hosted E2A text carries an explicit caveat, quoted verbatim: *"The time frames and definitions in this guideline differ from those in the Code of Federal Regulations [21 CFR 314.80]. Until the regulations are revised, the time frames and definitions in the CFR should be followed."* For a US-marketed product the CFR governs; for an IND safety report the applicable provision is 21 CFR 312.32. Paragraph-level citations to 21 CFR 314.80(c)(1) and 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1) are given for orientation only and **must be re-verified against the current eCFR text** before use; the numeric answers in §1 rest on the E2A passages quoted in §2, not on the CFR.
- **European Union.** E2A is adopted in the EU as CPMP/ICH/377/95 (legal effective date 1 June 1995). For interventional clinical trials conducted under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, SUSAR reporting time frames are set by that Regulation (Article 42) and its implementing acts; those provisions should be checked and cited at article level from the current consolidated text before this draft is finalised.
- **Other regions.** National implementing guidance (e.g. gateway, portal or paper channel, local follow-up rules, local language requirements) has not been retrieved and is not cited here. If the case falls in such a region, that guidance must be added to this draft before use.
- **Whether the case is investigational or marketed.** E2A is the investigational-phase standard. For a marketed product, the post-approval framework (and, in the US, the CFR as noted above) may impose different or additional obligations.

None of these overrides changes the E2A figures of 7 and 15; they determine whether the E2A figures are the ones that legally bind this particular case.

---

## 8. Audit documentation the sponsor should hold for this case

1. Evidence of the **day-0 determination**: the source document (e.g. initial notification from the site), the date and time it was first received by any sponsor personnel, and the identity of the recipient.
2. A signed statement that the four minimum criteria were met on that date, with the elements enumerated.
3. The **day-7** and **day-15** due dates calculated and recorded at the time of triage (not reconstructed later), using calendar-day arithmetic with day 0 excluded.
4. Transmission records: gateway/portal acknowledgement or fax/telephone record, with date and time, and the case identification number used on both submissions.
5. A record of any medically significant follow-up information received after the initial report and the re-started clock it triggers (E2D draft §3.2.2).

---

## 9. Limits of this draft

- The answers are stated for the population in §3 and the E2A framework; §7 lists the checks required before they can be relied on for a specific case.
- The day-0 counting convention is sourced to a **draft** ICH E2D text; confirm against the final E2D guideline and against local guidance.

**Question (ask 2).** A device meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 360j(b). Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21, must its manufacturer submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution?

**Answer: No.** 21 CFR 807.85(a) states, in terms: "A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act." Section 807.85 sits inside Subpart E, the same subpart that contains the 90-day rule in §807.81(a). A device that is within the meaning of §520(b) is therefore outside the class of devices for which §807.81(a) requires a premarket notification, and the 90-day advance-submission obligation in §807.81(a) does not attach to it.

**The answer is conditional, and the condition is substantive, not clerical.** The exemption in §807.85(a) is keyed to the device being "within the meaning of section 520(b)." If the device does not in fact satisfy every element of §520(b), or if it loses the exemption because a §520(b)(2) condition is not met, then §807.81(a) applies in full and the manufacturer **must** submit a premarket notification at least **90 days** before it proposes to begin introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution. > **V.A. From which premarket and postmarket requirements is my custom device exempt?** Under Section 520(b) of the FD&C Act, custom devices are exempt from Premarket Approval (PMA) requirements and conformance to mandatory performance standards. Custom Devices are not exempt from any other requirements, including, but not limited to, the Quality System Regulation, including Design Controls (21 CFR Part 820); Medical Device Reporting (21 CFR Part 803); Labeling (21 CFR Part 801); Corrections and Removals (21 CFR Part 806); and Registration and Listing (21 CFR Part 807).

> **V.B. ... Can a single custom device be unique both to a physician's practice and the patient's unique needs?** No, the custom device provision allows for development of two different categories of custom devices. One is patient-centric, and the other physician-centric; a custom device cannot be both patient- and physician-centric.

---

## 4. Reasoning

**Step 1 — §807.81(a) is the general rule and it is broad.** It reaches "each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20" and any device intended for human use that meets §807.81(a)(1), (a)(2) or (a)(3). A first-time commercial distributor of a novel device will ordinarily meet (a)(1) and (a)(2). Absent an exemption, the notification is due "at least 90 days before" the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

**Step 2 — §807.81(b) does not itself list custom devices.** The two carve-outs in §807.81(b)(1) are a pending PMA/reclassification petition and a cleared PCCP; §807.81(b)(2) is an exception/alternative mechanism under Parts 801/809. None of these is the custom-device route. The custom-device route is not a carve-out from §807.81 — it is a separate, express exemption located later in the same subpart.

**Step 3 — §807.85(a) is an express exemption from "premarket notification requirements of this subpart."** "This subpart" is Subpart E, i.e. the subpart that contains §807.81. The exemption is not limited to §807.81(a)(1) or to any particular criterion; it is an exemption from the subpart's premarket notification requirements as a class. Because the 90-day advance-submission obligation exists only as an element of §807.81(a), and §807.81(a) does not apply to an exempt device, there is no 90-day pre-commercial-distribution submission obligation for a device within the meaning of §520(b).

**Step 4 — the exemption is definitional, not discretionary.** §807.85(a) contains no FDA application, no request, no grant, and no pre-clearance step. It operates by the device's status: "if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b)." The burden of establishing and documenting that status rests on the manufacturer, and it is a documentation burden, not an approval burden. FDA's guidance confirms the exemption is not a broad safe harbor: it "does not create a broad, new exemption from sections" (S6, Background).

**Step 5 — the statutory exemption in §520(b)(1) is narrower than the regulatory notification exemption, and the two must not be conflated.** Section §520(b)(1) on its face disapplies only "the requirements of sections 514 and 515" (performance standards and premarket approval). It does not, by its own words, disapply section 510(k). The premarket-notification relief comes from §807.85(a), a regulation promulgated under the Act. This matters for the answer to ask 2: the reason the manufacturer need not file a 510(k) is §807.85(a), and that is precisely the provision the question puts in issue. The regulation is in force (last amended 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016) and unamended as of the retrieval date.

**Step 6 — no numeric conflict among the 90-day figures in Subpart E.** Three distinct 90-day periods appear in Subpart E and must not be used interchangeably:

| Period | Value | What it measures | Status for a §520(b) device |
|---|---|---|---|
| §807.81(a) advance-submission interval | at least **90 days** before proposed introduction/delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution | submitter's filing lead time | **Not applicable** — device exempt under §807.85(a) |
| FDA action period on a notification (section headed "FDA action on a premarket notification" in Subpart E) | **90 days** | FDA's review clock from receipt | Not reached — no notification filed |
| §807.95(b) confidentiality period for a not-yet-marketed device | **90 days** from date of receipt of the submission | public disclosure of the existence of a submission | Not reached — no submission exists |

The verdict in §1 turns on the first row only, and that row is inapplicable. The other two 90-day figures are noted so that no downstream reader assigns the wrong 90-day period to this device.

**Step 7 — the exemption is lost if a §520(b) condition fails, and loss is retroactive in effect.** S6 footnote 13 states that without submission of the required annual report, devices distributed as custom devices "would not be exempted from any applicable premarket requirements." "Any applicable premarket requirements" includes 510(k). Accordingly the correct full statement of the answer is: **no 510(k) is required, provided the device remains within §520(b) and the manufacturer satisfies §520(b)(2); if either fails, §807.81(a) requires the notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution.**

---

## 5. Conditions that preserve the "No" and conditions that convert it to "Yes"

This is the operative risk content of the analysis. Each row states the condition, the unit or threshold, and the consequence of failure.

| # | Condition (source) | Threshold / unit | If not met |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Device is created or modified to comply with the order of an individual physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person designated under regulations) — §520(b)(1)(A) | Categorical; requires a documented individual order | Not a custom device; §807.81(a) applies → notification ≥ **90 days** before commercial distribution |
| C2 | Compliance with that order necessarily deviates from an otherwise applicable §514 performance standard or §515 requirement — §520(b)(1)(B) | Categorical; requires identification of the specific standard/requirement deviated from | Not a custom device; §807.81(a) applies |
| C3 | Not generally available in the United States in finished form through labeling or advertising by the manufacturer, importer or distributor for commercial distribution — §520(b)(1)(C) | Categorical (no advertising/labeling offering the finished device for commercial distribution) | Not a custom device; §807.81(a) applies |
| C4 | Use limitation: intended for use by a **patient named in the order** of the physician/dentist (or other specially qualified person), **or** intended **solely for use by** a physician/dentist (or other specially qualified person) and not generally available to, or generally used by, other such persons — §807.85(a)(1)–(2) | Categorical; the two routes are mutually exclusive — a device cannot be both patient-centric and physician-centric (S6, Q&A V.B) | Not within §807.85(a); §807.81(a) applies |
| C5 | Quantity: device is "of a type available for introduction into commercial distribution in quantities of no more than five units per year" (S6, definition of "not generally available"; S6 Background: "not to exceed 5 units per year") | **≤ 5 units per device type per year** | Exceeds the custom-device quantity limit; device is generally available; §807.81(a) applies |
| C6 | Annual report to FDA on devices manufactured and distributed under §520(b) — §520(b)(2)(C), as described in S6 footnote 13 | Annual, one report per year; **exact due date not verified in the retrieved sources — see §7, step V2** | "Would not be exempted from any applicable premarket requirements" → §807.81(a) applies, notification ≥ **90 days** before commercial distribution |

**Practical reading of C5.** The 5-unit figure is a per-device-type, per-year ceiling, not a per-patient or per-order ceiling, and not a lifetime ceiling. A manufacturer that ships a 6th unit of the same device type in a calendar year has, on FDA's stated reading, a device that is generally available, and the exemption in §807.85(a) is not available for that device.

---

## 6. What the exemption does **not** do

A "No" to ask 2 is a narrow answer. Per §807.85(a) the relief is only from "premarket notification requirements of this subpart" (Subpart E), and per §520(b)(1) only from sections 514 and 515. Per S6 Q&A V.A, custom devices are **not** exempt from:

- Quality System Regulation, including Design Controls — 21 CFR Part 820;
- Medical Device Reporting — 21 CFR Part 803;
- Labeling — 21 CFR Part 801;
- Corrections and Removals — 21 CFR Part 806;
- **Registration and Listing — 21 CFR Part 807** (i.e. Subparts A and B of the same part; the §807.85(a) exemption reaches Subpart E only).

This is the single most likely misreading of the answer: "exempt from premarket notification" is not "exempt from Part 807." The establishment registration and device listing obligations in Part 807 Subparts A–B continue to apply, and §807.81(a) presupposes registration under §807.20 — the exemption removes the notification, not the registration.

---

## 7. Residual uncertainty and reviewer verification steps

| ID | Item | Why it matters | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | Text in force on **2026-11-21** specifically; sources retrieved 2026-11-23T04:32:11–12Z | 2-day window between as-of date and retrieval; no amendment appears in the history notes, but the window is not formally closed | Run eCFR point-in-time for 2026-11-21 on §§807.81 and 807.85; attach dated screenshot to file |
| V2 | Exact text and due date of the §520(b)(2)(C) annual report obligation | C6 is a condition of continued exemption (S6 fn. 13); a missed deadline forfeits the 510(k) exemption | Obtain the current FDA guidance *Custom Device Exemption* and the §520(b)(2) statutory text; confirm the reporting deadline and content; confirm the guidance's issue date and whether it has been revised or withdrawn as of 2026-11-21 |
| V3 | Full text of §520(b)(1)(D) | Not captured verbatim in the retrieved sources; §807.85(a)(1)–(2) is treated here as its operative restatement | Confirm (D) against the U.S. Code (21 U.S.C. 360j(b)) before relying on §3.3 as a complete statutory quotation |
| V4 | Device-specific classification | A device may independently be 510(k)-exempt by classification regulation; that is a separate and cumulative basis for "no notification," and its existence or absence does not change the §807.85(a) analysis but does change the file | Identify the classification regulation and product code; record whether 510(k) is required for the type |
| V5 | Whether the arrangement is genuinely patient-specific or physician-specific | C4; S6 Q&A V.B bars a device being both | Document which single route is claimed and the evidence for it |

---

## 8. Documentation checklist the manufacturer should be able to produce on inspection

For each device distributed under the §520(b) route, retain:

1. The individual physician's (or dentist's, or other specially qualified person's) **order**, identifying the **named patient** (patient-centric route) or the **physician's special need** (physician-centric route) — C1, C4.
2. A written statement of the **§514 performance standard or §515 requirement** from which the device necessarily deviates to comply with that order — C2.
3. Evidence that the device is **not** offered in finished form through labeling or advertising for commercial distribution in the United States — C3.
4. A **unit ledger by device type and calendar year** showing cumulative units introduced into commercial distribution, capped at **5 units per device type per year** — C5.
5. The **annual report** submitted to FDA under §520(b)(2)(C), with proof and date of submission — C6.
6. Confirmation of **establishment registration and device listing** under 21 CFR Part 807 Subparts A–B, plus QSR, MDR, labeling and corrections/removals compliance — §6 above.
7. A dated copy of §§807.81 and 807.85 as in force on the relevant distribution date — V1.

---

## 9. Bottom line, restated in one sentence

Under 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, a device that is within the meaning of FD&C Act §520(b) is exempt from the subpart's premarket notification requirements by operation of §807.85(a), so its manufacturer need **not** submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution — unless and until the device falls outside §520(b) (including by exceeding **5 units per device type per year**, by becoming generally available in finished form, by lacking the requisite individual order, or by failure to submit the §520(b)(2)(C) annual report), at which point §807.81(a) requires the notification at least **90 days** before introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

---

Regulatory interpretation depends on facts about the specific device, its orders, its distribution and its advertising that are not in the record here; the conclusion in §1 is conditional on those facts as set out in §5.*
