# Does the CDC stated preference for TB blood tests apply to a 4-year-old BCG vaccine recipient?

## 1. Source (ask 1 — constraint satisfied)
Primary source reviewed, and the only source used for the applicability verdict:
- Title: Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis (For Health Care Providers)
- Publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
- URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/
- Page revision date printed on page: Apr. 17, 2025
- Retrieved (harness fetch): 2026-11-23T04:35:55Z; retrieval sha256: 9095c1db7f3e
- Requested reference date: 2026-11-21
Limitation of this citation, stated plainly: the retrieved copy carries a fetch timestamp of 2026-11-23, i.e. 2 days after the reference date of 2026-11-21 named in the request. The page's own revision date is Apr. 17, 2025 and there is no evidence of any edit between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23, so the content quoted below is the content available on 2026-11-21 to the best of available evidence; a 2026-11-21 archived snapshot has not been independently verified.

Secondary CDC pages cited only for transparency about internal CDC wording (NOT used to change the verdict): CDC, Tuberculosis Clinical Care for Children, https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html, page date Apr. 17, 2025, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:55Z (sha256 171f6557d84e); CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Interferon Gamma Release Assay, https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/interferon-gamma-release-assay.html, page date May 9, 2024, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:55Z (sha256 4791076e7908); CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:54Z (sha256 4aa43e3065d3); CDC, Tuberculosis in Children (public page), https://www.cdc.gov/tb/about/children.html, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:55Z (sha256 de6543e1f048).

## 2. Case as specified in the request
- Population: one child, age 4 years (i.e., 4 years of age; below the 5 years of age boundary discussed by the source).
- Exposure of interest: prior receipt of Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine (dose and date not specified in the request; TB vaccine given in infancy per CDC's public page).
- Setting: U.S. clinical context in which CDC guidance applies (assumption stated in project context).
- Assumed unless corrected: the child is otherwise healthy/immunocompetent; no prior positive TB test; no stated TB symptoms; no stated TB exposure. The indication for testing (screening vs. exposure investigation vs. symptoms) was not specified in the request and is flagged in §5.
- Units: age in years; TST reaction sizes, where quoted by the source, in millimeters (mm) of induration.

## 3. What the named CDC page states (verbatim)
From https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/ (Apr. 17, 2025):

(a) Under 'TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])': "Only one visit is required to draw blood for the test. TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine."

(b) Under 'TB skin test (Mantoux tuberculin skin test)': "TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome. Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance1 on the use of TB blood tests in children."

(c) FDA-approved blood tests named on the page: "QuantiFERON®-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus)" and "T-SPOT®.TB test (T-Spot)"; qualitative QFT-Plus results are "reported as positive, negative, or indeterminate"; "Laboratories should provide both the qualitative and quantitative results."

## 4. Application to this child — explicit statement vs. inference
Explicit in the source (not inference): the stated preference for TB blood tests is bounded to "people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine" (quote (a)).
Explicit in the source (not inference): for "children younger than 5 years of age," "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing" (quote (b)).
Arithmetic comparison (transparent, not inference about clinical meaning): child age = 4 years; stated blood-test preference lower bound = 5 years of age; 4 years < 5 years. The child is outside the age band of the stated preference and inside the 'younger than 5 years of age' band for which the page states TST is the recommended method.
Inference (labeled as such): because the stated preference is conditional on both (i) BCG receipt and (ii) age ≥5 years, and this child meets (i) but not (ii), the stated preference on this page does not extend to this child.

VERDICT (ask 2): No. On the CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' page (Apr. 17, 2025), the stated preference for TB blood tests applies to people 5 years of age and older who received BCG vaccine; a 4-year-old (4 years of age) does not meet that stated age criterion, and the same page states that current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age.

## 5. Qualifications the reviewing clinician must weigh (all source-anchored)
1. The page itself preserves a pediatric caveat that must not be lost when reading the verdict: it notes "that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children" and that providers "may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children" (quote (b)). The verdict answers only what this CDC page's stated preference says; it is not a statement that IGRA is prohibited or clinically wrong in a 4-year-old.
2. Internal CDC wording differs across CDC pages, and the reviewer should be aware of the tension (this does not change the verdict, which is grounded in the named page): the Tuberculin Skin Test guidance page states "BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children" (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:54Z) — an unqualified-by-age 'including children' statement. The IGRA guidance page states the blood-test preference for "People who have received the BCG vaccine" but immediately qualifies: "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age... The collection of a sufficient blood sample can be a practical barrier to testing very young children with a TB blood test" (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/interferon-gamma-release-assay.html, page date May 9, 2024, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:55Z). The children's clinical-care page states the age-bounded rule: "Health care providers should recommend the TB blood test if a child: Is five years of age or older and Has ever received the BCG vaccine (TB vaccine)." (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html, Apr. 17, 2025, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:55Z). The requested source page's own two statements (§3a and §3b) are mutually consistent with each other and with the ≥5 years of age rule.
3. BCG and TST cross-reactivity, as stated on the children's clinical-care page: "The BCG vaccine may cause a false-positive TB skin test reaction. There is no reliable way to distinguish a positive TB skin test reaction caused by BCG vaccination from a reaction caused by true TB infection. Interpretation of the TB skin test reaction is the same for people who have had BCG vaccination as it is for those who have not." (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html). The TST guidance page adds: "tuberculin reactivity is likely during the first two years after BCG administration to the newborn" and that "[m]ultiple BCG doses... increases a person's sensitivity to the TB skin test and the duration of positive TB skin test results after BCG administration." Units: time in years; number of doses in doses. This is the mechanistic rationale a reviewer may weigh when choosing IGRA off-label for a BCG-vaccinated 4-year-old, but it is not the stated preference of the named page.
4. Indication for testing was not specified in the request. Per the named page, "CDC recommends testing people who are at increased risk for TB infection" and "CDC discourages a testing approach that is independent of a risk assessment." If the trigger is exposure to a person with TB disease, the children's clinical-care page adds: "Children less than five years of age who have spent time with an adult with TB disease should receive treatment for latent TB infection even if the initial TB blood test or TB skin test result is negative and less than eight to 10 weeks have passed since the child's last exposure to TB disease. This is called window prophylaxis." Units: age in years; interval in weeks (8–10 weeks since last exposure). This materially affects management and must be supplied by the clinician.
5. Test-type caveat for whichever test is used: a positive result "usually means TB infection" and "[m]ore tests, such as a chest radiograph, are needed to rule out TB disease"; "Some people with TB disease may have a negative TB blood test or TB skin test result" (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/clinical-and-laboratory-diagnosis.html, fetched 2026-11-23T04:35:54Z). QFT-Plus qualitative results include 'indeterminate' (named page, quote (c)); the request did not supply indeterminate-result rates for young children and none are asserted here.
6. Per the TST guidance page, both test types "should not be performed on people who have written documentation of a previous positive TB test result (TB blood test or TB skin test) or treatment for TB disease." Prior-test history for this child was not supplied.

# NICE guideline identification and lineage for primary hypertension in adults (including adults with type 2 diabetes)

**Status: draft evidence note for review by a qualified clinician. Not medical advice. Not for patient care or for direct application to any individual. No dose or exposure figures are given in this note because the ask is guideline identification and lineage only; any pathway content added later must state population, dose or exposure, and units for every figure.**

---

## 1. Direct answers

### Ask 1 — Which NICE guideline covers the scope (identifying and treating primary hypertension in adults, including adults with type 2 diabetes)?

**NG136 — NICE guideline 'Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management', reference number NG136. Published 28 August 2019; last updated 26 February 2026 (as shown on the guideline page when retrieved 23 November 2026).**

The scope match is word-for-word, quoted from the NG136 overview page:

> "This guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (high blood pressure) in people aged 18 and over, including people with type 2 diabetes. It aims to reduce the risk of cardiovascular problems such as heart attacks and strokes by helping healthcare professionals to diagnose hypertension accurately and treat it effectively."
> — NICE (2019, last updated 2026) *Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management* (NG136), Overview. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/ (retrieved 23 November 2026).

The guideline's own list of what it makes recommendations on (same page) confirms the treatment scope the team needs:

> "This guideline includes recommendations on: diagnosing hypertension; starting antihypertensive drug treatment; monitoring treatment and blood pressure targets; choosing antihypertensive drug treatment (treatment steps 1 to 4); measuring blood pressure; assessing cardiovascular risk and target organ damage; lifestyle interventions"
> — NICE (2019, last updated 2026) NG136, Recommendations (contents list). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/

Population: adults aged 18 and over, with or without type 2 diabetes. This note states no dose or exposure values; the guideline's drug-treatment steps are named only as section headings, not reproduced as prescribing content.

### Ask 2 — Which earlier NICE hypertension guideline does NG136 say it updates and replaces?

**CG127.**

Quoted verbatim from the NG136 overview page:

> "This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127. It also updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in the NICE guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28)."
> — NICE (2019, last updated 2026) NG136, Overview. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/ (retrieved 23 November 2026).

And from the NG136 full-guideline PDF, the short-form replacement statements on the copyright/imprint page:

> "This guideline replaces CG127."
> "This guideline partially replaces NG28."
> — NICE (2019, last updated 2026) *Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management* (NG136), full guideline PDF. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-managementpdf-66141722710213

**CG127 is the answer to ask 2** because it is the earlier NICE *hypertension* guideline named in NG136's replacement statement. NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults: management) is also affected, but only its blood-pressure-management section, and NG28 is a diabetes guideline rather than an earlier hypertension guideline — so it is recorded below as a secondary lineage fact, not as the answer to ask 2.

**Verification note on CG127 (deliberate limitation).** The fetched passages identify CG127 by reference number only. No fetched passage gives CG127's full title or its publication month. NG136's Context section refers to "the publication of the 2011 NICE guideline on hypertension", which corroborates that CG127 is the 2011 hypertension guideline, but the title and exact publication date must be read off the NICE CG127 page and pasted into this note before the pathway is signed off. Do not let a writer 'fill in' a CG127 title or date from memory.

---

## 2. Secondary lineage fact the pathway team needs (type 2 diabetes boundary)

Because the team's scope explicitly includes adults with type 2 diabetes, the NG28 interaction matters and is often mis-stated. The position, in NICE's own words:

- NG136 *partially* replaces NG28 — specifically the blood-pressure-management section:
  > "This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127. It also updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in the NICE guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28)." — NG136 Overview.
- NG28 has removed its own hypertension recommendations and redirects to NG136:
  > "1.44 Diagnosing and managing hypertension — The recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension have been removed. For recommendations on hypertension in people with type 2 diabetes, see NICE's guideline on hypertension in adults. Diagnosis, treatment and monitoring of hypertension is broadly the same for people with type 2 diabetes as for other people. When a different approach is needed for people with type 2 diabetes, this is specified in the hypertension guideline."
  > — NICE *Type 2 diabetes in adults: management* (NG28), full guideline PDF, section 1.44. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28/resources/type-2-diabetes-in-adults-management-pdf-1837338615493
- NG28's update log records when this happened:
  > "August 2019: The recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension have been removed because diagnosis, treatment and monitoring of hypertension is broadly the same for people with type 2 diabetes as for other people (see the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults). When a different approach is needed for people with type 2 diabetes, this is specified in the hypertension guideline."
  > — NICE NG28, full guideline PDF, Update information.
- NG28's overview repeats the redirect:
  > "For recommendations on hypertension in people with type 2 diabetes, see the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults."
  > — NICE *Type 2 diabetes in adults: management* (NG28), Overview. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG28
- Two recommendations now living in NG136 were originally NG28 section 1.4 content — relevant if the team is de-duplicating its diabetes and hypertension pathways:
  > "Recommendations 1.2.12 and 1.4.24 (marked [2009]) were originally published in section 1.4 of NICE's guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults, which was updated by this guideline."
  > — NICE NG136, Update information. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Update-information
- NG136 states explicitly that its drug-treatment section spans both populations:
  > "Choosing antihypertensive drug treatment (for people with or without type 2 diabetes) — The recommendations in this section apply to people with hypertension with or without type 2 diabetes. They replace the recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension in NICE's guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults. For guidance on choosing antihypertensive drug treatment in people with type 1 diabetes, see also the section on control of cardiovascular risk in NICE's guideline on type 1 diabetes."
  > — NICE NG136, full guideline PDF.

**Practical consequence for the pathway:** there should be one hypertension pathway (NG136) that names type 2 diabetes where NG136 itself differentiates, and no parallel hypertension section copied from NG28. NG28 retains the diabetes-specific content (glycaemic management, cardiovascular risk, complications) but no longer owns blood pressure diagnosis or drug treatment.

**Out of scope but must be signposted, not merged:** NG136 states "NICE has also produced a guideline on hypertension in pregnancy" (NG136 Overview). Pregnancy hypertension is a separate guideline and must not be folded into this pathway. Secondary hypertension is also outside NG136's stated scope, which is *primary* hypertension.

# Informed consent, 'minimal risk', and 21 CFR Part 50 — regulatory analysis

**Status of this document.** Draft regulatory analysis prepared for review by a qualified clinician and by regulatory affairs. It is not medical advice and must not be used to make an enrollment decision. Every regulatory statement below is tied to a section of 21 CFR Part 50 (or a named cross-referenced part) with its source note, and the version relied on is stated in Section 2.

**Prepared against:** 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21 (constraint supplied with the request).

---

## 1. Questions and short answers

**Q1 (constraint).** Analysis is to be conducted under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21. Basis for the text used is set out in Section 2.

**Q2 (verdict). Is 'the research is minimal risk' alone a sufficient basis for an FDA-regulated clinical investigation to enroll a person without informed consent?**

**No.** Minimal risk is a *necessary* condition of the one Part 50 provision that permits a consent waiver on minimal-risk grounds (21 CFR 50.22, added at 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023), but it is not a *sufficient* one. Section 50.22 requires the IRB to find and document five separate elements, of which minimal risk is only the first. An investigator's own conclusion that a study is minimal risk is not a waiver of consent, and the other two exceptions in Part 50 (§ 50.23 and § 50.24) are not available on minimal-risk grounds at all.

**Q3 (value). How does Part 50 define minimal risk?**

21 CFR 50.3(k): *"Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests."* Parsed in Section 4.

---

## 2. Text in force on 2026-11-21 — what was verified and what remains to be verified

Sources consulted:

- eCFR, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter A, Part 50, including §§ 50.22, 50.23, 50.24 and the Part 50 landing page. Retrieved 2026-11-23T04:42:40Z; page hashes 8f4718b5053d (§ 50.22), 7566e7f06250 (§ 50.23), 721cc8b321ca (§ 50.24), 2f071d1f35d8 (Part 50).
- U.S. Government Publishing Office, *CFR 2025, Title 21, Volume 1, Part 50* (edition as of 2025-04-01); page hash c34db2d44ed7.
- U.S. Government Publishing Office, XML for 21 CFR 50.24, *CFR 2025, Title 21, Volume 1*; page hash 22661ce48877.

What these establish:

1. Section 50.22 exists in both the 2025 print edition and the eCFR, carrying the source note **[88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023]**. It is therefore codified and in force well before 2026-11-21.
2. The Part 50 table of contents in the 2025 edition lists Subpart B as §§ 50.20, 50.22, 50.23, 50.24, 50.25, 50.27, and shows Subpart C as **[Reserved]** — i.e. no separate consent regime for pregnant women, fetuses or neonates exists within Part 50 itself.
3. The minimal-risk sentence quoted in Section 4 appears identically in both snapshots, and no source note later than 88 FR 88248 attaches to §§ 50.20, 50.22, 50.23, 50.24 or 50.3 in either snapshot.

What remains to be verified before reliance: the eCFR retrieval is timestamped 2026-11-23, two days after the requested in-force date of 2026-11-21. The retrieved text shows no amendment with an effective date falling between those two dates, and the conclusion in Section 1 does not turn on any such amendment, but a **point-in-time eCFR query pinned to 2026-11-21** should be run for §§ 50.3, 50.20, 50.22, 50.23 and 50.24, and the section-level hashes filed with the study documentation. If the pinned query returns different text, this analysis must be re-run. The verdict in Section 1 would change only if § 50.22's five findings were reduced or § 50.20's consent gate were removed; neither snapshot shows that.

---

## 3. Why 'minimal risk' alone is not sufficient — the structure of Part 50

### 3.1 Consent is the default rule, and the exceptions are enumerated

21 CFR 50.20: *"Except as provided in §§ 50.22, 50.23, and 50.24, no investigator may involve a human being as a subject in research covered by these regulations unless the investigator has obtained the legally effective informed consent of the subject or the subject's legally authorized representative."*

Three consequences follow directly from that sentence. First, informed consent is the default obligation. Second, the only exceptions within Part 50 are §§ 50.22, 50.23 and 50.24 — there are exactly three. Third, each of the three is a *conditional* exception: none is phrased as 'if the research is minimal risk, consent is not required.'

### 3.2 Section 50.22 is the only minimal-risk exception, and it is a five-element test the IRB must find and document

21 CFR 50.22, in full (source note [88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023]):

> *"The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation described in this section may approve an informed consent procedure that does not include or that alters some or all of the elements of informed consent set forth in § 50.25(a) and (b), or may waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following:*
>
> *(a) The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;*
>
> *(b) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration;*
>
> *(c) If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format;*
>
> *(d) The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects; and*
>
> *(e) Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation."*

Three points of construction:

- **Minimal risk is one of five findings, not the test.** Paragraph (a) is the minimal-risk finding. Paragraphs (b), (d) and (e) apply to every § 50.22 waiver. Paragraph (c) applies additionally whenever identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are used. A study that is minimal risk but that could practicably be carried out with consent fails at (b); a study that is minimal risk but whose waiver would adversely affect subjects' rights and welfare fails at (d).
- **The finding belongs to the IRB, not the investigator.** The operative subject of § 50.22 is *"The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation,"* and the operative verb is *"finds and documents."* An investigator's, sponsor's or statistician's own minimal-risk judgment has no effect on the § 50.20 default.
- **The waiver is of the consent requirement or of § 50.25(a) and (b) elements — nothing else.** It does not waive IRB review and approval under 21 CFR Part 56, IND/IDE obligations under 21 CFR Parts 312 and 812, the additional elements in § 50.25(c) (not named in § 50.22), Subpart D for children (Section 3.5), or any applicable state or local law.

**Therefore: minimal risk alone is insufficient.** Where an IRB has made and documented all five findings, enrollment without consent is permitted; where it has not, enrollment without consent violates § 50.20.

### 3.3 Section 50.23 is not available on minimal-risk grounds

21 CFR 50.23(a): *"The obtaining of informed consent shall be deemed feasible unless, before use of the test article (except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section), both the investigator and a physician who is not otherwise participating in the clinical investigation certify in writing all of the following: (1) The human subject is confronted by a life-threatening situation necessitating the use of the test article. (2) Informed consent cannot be obtained from the subject because of an inability to communicate with, or obtain legally effective consent from, the subject. (3) Time is not sufficient to obtain consent from the subject's legal representative. (4) There is available no alternative method of approved or generally recognized therapy that provides an equal or greater likelihood of saving the life of the subject."*

This pathway is structurally the opposite of a minimal-risk study: it presupposes a life-threatening situation, an incapacitated subject, an insufficient therapeutic window, and absence of equivalent approved therapy, and it requires contemporaneous written certification by two physicians. A minimal-risk study satisfies none of these conditions and cannot use § 50.23.

The other pathways within § 50.23 are likewise inapplicable: § 50.23(d) implements the Presidential waiver for members of the armed forces under 10 U.S.C. 1107(f) (*"the President may waive the prior consent requirement for the administration of an investigational new drug to a member of the armed forces in connection with the member's participation in a particular military operation"*), and § 50.23(e) addresses investigational in vitro diagnostic devices used to identify chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear agents in a *"life-threatening situation."* Neither is a minimal-risk route. Paragraphs (b) and (c) of § 50.23 were not captured in the source passages used for this draft, are not relied on here, and should be read from the in-force text before any § 50.23-based plan is considered. Section 50.23 also imposes a written-certification obligation and a duty to submit that documentation to the IRB; the reporting interval is stated in the section and should be quoted from the in-force text rather than paraphrased.

### 3.4 Section 50.24 is not available on minimal-risk grounds

21 CFR 50.24(a) permits an IRB, *"with the concurrence of a licensed physician who is a member of or consultant to the IRB and who is not otherwise participating in the clinical investigation,"* to approve an investigation without requiring consent of all subjects only if it finds and documents **each** of the following:

- **(a)(1)** *"The human subjects are in a life-threatening situation, available treatments are unproven or unsatisfactory, and the collection of valid scientific evidence, which may include evidence obtained through randomized placebo-controlled investigations, is necessary to determine the safety and effectiveness of particular interventions."*
- **(a)(2)** Consent is not feasible because *(i)* subjects cannot consent as a result of their medical condition, *(ii)* the intervention must be administered before consent from legally authorized representatives is feasible, and *(iii)* *"There is no reasonable way to identify prospectively the individuals likely to become eligible for participation in the clinical investigation."*
- **(a)(3)** Participation holds out the prospect of direct benefit because subjects face a life-threatening situation, appropriate animal and other preclinical studies support potential direct benefit, and the risks are reasonable in relation to the condition, standard therapy and the proposed intervention.
- **(a)(4)** *"The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the waiver."*

Section 50.24(a)(5) adds community consultation with representatives of the communities from which subjects will be drawn, *"public disclosure to the communities in which the clinical investigation will be conducted and from which the subjects will be drawn, prior to initiation of the clinical investigation, of plans for the investigation and its risks and expected benefits,"* public disclosure of results after completion, *"Establishment of an independent data monitoring committee to exercise oversight of the clinical investigation,"* and, where consent is not feasible and no legally authorized representative is reasonably available, a commitment to attempt contact with a family member within the therapeutic window and to ask whether that person objects. Section 50.24(c) requires the IRB to retain the paragraph (a) determinations and the related documentation *"for at least 3 years after completion of the clinical investigation."* Section 50.24(d) requires the protocol to be conducted under a **separate IND or IDE** that identifies it as a protocol that may include subjects who are unable to consent, and forbids submission as an amendment under §§ 312.30 or 812.35. Section 50.24 also requires that procedures be in place to inform each subject, or a legally authorized representative or family member, at the earliest feasible opportunity, of inclusion in the investigation and of the right to discontinue.

Every one of these conditions is foreign to a minimal-risk study. A study that is minimal risk cannot be routed through § 50.24, and § 50.24 does not require minimal risk — emergency research is typically greater than minimal risk.

### 3.5 Children: Subpart D is an additional overlay that a § 50.22 waiver does not remove

21 CFR 50.51: *"Any clinical investigation within the scope described in §§ 50.1 and 56.101 of this chapter in which no greater than minimal risk to children is presented may involve children as subjects only if the IRB finds that: (a) No greater than minimal risk to children is presented; and (b) Adequate provisions are made for soliciting the assent of the children and the permission of their parents or guardians as set forth in § 50.55."* (Source note [78 FR 12951, Feb. 26, 2013].) Sections 50.52 and 50.53 then govern greater-than-minimal-risk pediatric research with and without prospect of direct benefit.

Subpart D is captioned *"Additional Safeguards for Children in Clinical Investigations."* Nothing in § 50.22 states that it displaces Subpart D. The conservative and, in this draft's view, correct reading is that a § 50.22 waiver of consent does not by itself authorize enrollment of a child without the § 50.55 permission of parents or guardians; the IRB must separately satisfy § 50.51 (or § 50.52/50.53 as applicable) including the assent and permission findings. **This is an interpretive position and should be confirmed with FDA or institutional counsel before any pediatric enrollment.**

### 3.6 What the investigator's statement most likely reflects

- **Conflation with the Common Rule.** Under 45 CFR 46.116(f) a minimal-risk waiver has long been available for research not subject to FDA regulation. Before the 2023 addition of § 50.22, Part 50 contained no codified minimal-risk waiver and FDA relied on an enforcement-discretion position (described in FDA's July 2017 guidance, *IRB Waiver or Alteration of Informed Consent for Clinical Investigations Involving No More Than Minimal Risk to Human Subjects*). The 2023 rule codified the authority and harmonized it with 46.116(f), but as an FDA regulation requiring the five IRB findings. Whether the 2017 guidance remains in effect as of 2026-11-21 should be confirmed on FDA's guidance database; it does not change the analysis, because § 50.22 now supplies the authority and its conditions.
- **Treating § 50.3(k) as an exception.** It is a definition in Subpart A; it confers no waiver authority (Section 4).
- **Treating expedited IRB review under 21 CFR 56.110 as a consent waiver.** Review category and consent requirement are separate determinations.
- **Treating an investigator's or sponsor's risk determination as binding on the IRB.** It is not; § 50.22 assigns the finding to the IRB.
- **Assuming a waiver granted for one study extends to another.** Each IRB approval under § 50.22 is investigation-specific and must be re-found at continuing review, because § 50.22 refers to *"the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation."*
- **Assuming a procedure-specific waiver exists.** The Part 50 text retrieved contains no waiver keyed to a particular minimal-risk procedure (for example, a single blood draw). The only route is § 50.22 and its five findings.

---

## 4. The definition of minimal risk — 21 CFR 50.3(k)

Verbatim (identical in the eCFR and CFR 2025 snapshots):

> **"Minimal risk** means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests."

Element-by-element parsing, with what the IRB must therefore document:

1. **Two quantities — probability and magnitude.** Both the likelihood and the severity of the anticipated harm or discomfort must be no greater than the benchmark. A very probable but trivial harm (e.g. transient bruising) can be minimal; a very improbable but catastrophic harm generally cannot be.
2. **"anticipated in the research."** The assessment is prospective and applies to the research procedures as written in the protocol — not to the underlying disease, not to the standard care the subject would otherwise receive, and not to harms that occur outside the research.
3. **"not greater in and of themselves."** The comparison is between the research procedure and the benchmark, not net of any prospect of direct benefit. A research procedure does not become 'minimal risk' because the subject might benefit from it. (Sections 50.52 and 50.53 use a different, benefit-sensitive structure for children; that is a separate analysis and does not modify § 50.3(k).)
4. **Two benchmarks joined by 'or'.** Either (A) *"those ordinarily encountered in daily life"* or (B) *"during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests."* The disjunction means a procedure may qualify under either benchmark.
5. **'Daily life' — whose?** Part 50 does not say. Two readings are in circulation: the **general-population** reading (the daily life of an ordinary person) and the **subject-specific** reading (the daily life of persons with the subject's condition — for a person on chronic hemodialysis, routine venipuncture is part of daily life). FDA has not codified which applies. The choice is outcome-determinative: the subject-specific reading qualifies more procedures than the general-population reading. **Recommendation:** for a § 50.22 waiver, apply the general-population benchmark unless the IRB documents a reasoned basis for the subject-specific one, because the waiver removes the subject's own consent; and in either case record in the IRB minutes which benchmark was applied and why.
6. **'Routine' examinations or tests.** Routine means routine — performed at the frequency, invasiveness and setting of ordinary clinical practice. A test that is itself routine but is performed more often, more invasively, or for research purposes only may exceed the benchmark.
7. **It is a definition, not an authorization.** Section 50.3 sits in Subpart A (General Provisions) and supplies the meaning of 'minimal risk' wherever the term appears in Part 50 — including § 50.22(a), § 50.25(a)(6) (the injury-compensation disclosure applies only to *"research involving more than minimal risk"*), and §§ 50.51, 50.52 and 50.53. It authorizes nothing.
8. **What the definition does not supply.** There is no numerical threshold, no list of permitted procedures, and no definition of *"practicably"* (used in § 50.22(b)) in either § 50.3 or § 50.22. The IRB must document its practicability finding on the facts of the investigation; the interpretive sources are the FDA final-rule preamble at 88 FR 88248 (Dec. 21, 2023) and the Common Rule preamble at 82 FR 7149 (Jan. 19, 2017), both of which should be quoted directly in the IRB submission.

---

## 5. What the investigator must actually produce — a § 50.22 submission package

An investigator who believes the study qualifies should not enroll without consent on that belief. The deliverable is an IRB submission requesting a § 50.22 waiver or alteration, containing a documented finding for each element. Minimum content:

**§ 50.22(a) — no more than minimal risk.** A procedure-by-procedure risk table. For each procedure give: what is done, the number of times, the volume or dose **with units**, the probability and magnitude of each anticipated harm or discomfort, the benchmark applied (daily life, or routine examination/test), and the comparison. Example row format (the investigator supplies each estimate and its source; this draft supplies no risk estimates):

| Procedure | Frequency × amount (units) | Anticipated harm/discomfort | Probability | Magnitude | Benchmark applied | No greater than benchmark? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| e.g. Venipuncture | 1 × 10 mL whole blood | bruising, pain | (investigator estimate + source) | (grade/description) | routine physical examination | yes/no + rationale |

**§ 50.22(b) — practicability.** Why the investigation could not practicably be carried out with consent: the specific operational or scientific reason (for example, the eligible population cannot be prospectively identified or contacted; the number needed; the bias consent would introduce), with supporting evidence, and why alternatives (consent, altered consent, consent for a subset) were rejected.

**§ 50.22(c) — identifiable information or biospecimens (only if applicable).** Why the investigation could not practicably be carried out using de-identified information or biospecimens, and what identifiers are required and for how long.

**§ 50.22(d) — rights and welfare.** Privacy and confidentiality protections, the effect of the waiver on the subjects' ability to refuse or withdraw, treatment of vulnerable populations, and any data monitoring arrangements.

**§ 50.22(e) — post-participation information.** The plan for providing additional pertinent information after participation, or a documented justification for why it is not appropriate.

**Supporting documentation.** IRB minutes recording each of the five findings expressly and separately; the IRB-approved consent procedure or waiver; Part 56 records (21 CFR 56.115, which § 50.24(c) cross-references for record accessibility); the protocol's informed-consent section citing § 50.22; and, where the study is under an IND or IDE, the corresponding protocol documentation in that submission. Where the study is also subject to 45 CFR 46, the same submission should record the corresponding 46.116(f) findings so the two records are consistent.

---

## 6. Limits of this analysis

- The point-in-time confirmation described in Section 2 (eCFR query pinned to 2026-11-21) has not been run; the text used is the closest available and is consistent across two independent snapshots.
- The current status, as of 2026-11-21, of FDA's July 2017 minimal-risk waiver guidance and of any guidance issued after the 2023 rule should be confirmed on FDA's guidance database; it does not affect the verdict.
- The Subpart D position in Section 3.5 is an interpretation and is flagged as such.
- Whether 45 CFR 46 also applies, and which version of the Common Rule the relevant department has adopted, depends on the funding and the institution and is not resolved here.
- State and local law may impose consent requirements that a § 50.22 waiver does not satisfy; that is outside the scope of Part 50 and must be checked separately.
